spec.full_target: Let n,m be positive integers. Let u:R^n×(0,∞)→R^m be jointly smooth, and let q∈R^m have Euclidean norm one. Assume (i) |u(x,r)|=1 for all x,r>0; (ii) for each x,r>0 there exists a∈R with u_tt(x,r)-Δ_xu(x,r)=a u(x,r); (iii) on every compact time interval J⊂(0,∞), there is compact C_J⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q for x∉C_J and r∈J. Define e(x,r)=|u_t(x,r)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,r)|² and E(r)=∫_{R^n}e(x,r)dx with Lebesgue measure and Euclidean norms. Prove e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable for every r>0, E is differentiable at every r>0, and E'(r)=0.
spec.conclusion: For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable; E is differentiable at r and E'(r)=0.

parameters.type: vector in R^m with Euclidean norm one

hypotheses.statement: For every x∈R^n and r>0, |u(x,r)|=1, where |·| is the Euclidean norm.
For every x∈R^n and r>0 there exists a∈R such that u_tt(x,r)-Δ_xu(x,r)=a u(x,r), with Δ_x the componentwise spatial Laplacian.
For every compact interval J⊂(0,∞) there is a compact C_J⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q whenever x∉C_J and r∈J.

definitions.type: spatial componentwise Laplacian on R^m-valued maps

calculations: Finite sums and Euclidean inner-product differentiation; one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus; uniform convergence on compact boxes; Fubini for continuous compactly supported functions.

primitives.meaning: the real field with its usual topology, order, and Lebesgue measure
k-dimensional real Euclidean space with Lebesgue measure and Euclidean inner product

propositions.statement: For every x∈R^n and r>0, |u(x,r)|=1, where |·| is the Euclidean norm.
For every x∈R^n and r>0 there exists a∈R such that u_tt(x,r)-Δ_xu(x,r)=a u(x,r), with Δ_x the componentwise spatial Laplacian.
For every compact interval J⊂(0,∞) there is a compact C_J⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q whenever x∉C_J and r∈J.
For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable; E is differentiable at r and E'(r)=0.

argument.text: Fix r0>0 and choose a compact interval J⊂(0,∞) having r0 in its interior. By H003 choose compact C_J. For r∈J, u=q on the open complement of C_J, so all first derivatives vanish there; continuity makes them vanish on the boundary too. Thus e(·,r) is continuous, bounded on C_J and zero outside C_J, hence Lebesgue integrable. Choose a closed box B containing C_J. For r near r0, E(r)=∫_B e(x,r)dx. Smoothness gives continuous e_t on B×J, uniformly continuous there. The fundamental theorem of calculus expresses the difference quotient of e at r0 as the θ∈[0,1] average of e_t(x,r0+θh); uniform continuity gives uniform convergence in x∈B to e_t(x,r0). Since B has finite measure, integrating the difference quotients proves E'(r0)=∫_B e_t(x,r0)dx. Differentiate the finite sum defining e: e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j u_j·∂_j u_t. For each j, u_t·u_j is smooth and compactly supported; integrating its x_j derivative over R^n gives zero by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini, since that derivative is continuous and compactly supported. Therefore ∫(∂_j u_t)·u_j=−∫u_t·u_jj and E'(r0)=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu). Differentiating |u|²=1 in time yields u·u_t=0. By H002, u_tt−Δ_xu=a u pointwise for some scalar a, so u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=0. Hence E'(r0)=0. Since r0 was arbitrary, the target follows.
